:::{#thm-pd-invertible}
#### A positive definite matrix is invertible

Every positive definite matrix (@def-positive-definite) is invertible (@def-invertible-matrix).

:::

::: proof

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ positive definite matrix,
and let $\vx$ be a vector of length $p$ with $\matr{A} \vx = \vzero_p$.
Then

$$
\ba
\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx}
&= \tp{\vx}\,(\matr{A} \vx)
&& \text{(@def-quadratic-form)}
\\
&= \tp{\vx}\,\vzero_p
&& \text{(} \matr{A} \vx = \vzero_p \text{)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(every term of the inner product is } 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

If $\vx \ne \vzero_p$, then $\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} > 0$ because $\matr{A}$ is positive definite,
which contradicts $\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx} = 0$.
So $\vx = \vzero_p$, the null space $\mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$ is $\cb{\vzero_p}$,
and $\matr{A}$ is invertible by @thm-invertible-rank.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pd-invertible}
#### An invertible matrix that is not positive definite

$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ is positive definite, since

$$
\ba
\qform{\matr{A}}{\vx}
&= 2 x_1^2 + 2 x_1 x_2 + 2 x_2^2
&& \text{(multiply out)}
\\
&= x_1^2 + x_2^2 + (x_1 + x_2)^2,
&& \text{(expand the square)}
\ea
$$

which is $0$ only when $x_1 = x_2 = 0$.
It is invertible, with $\inv{\matr{A}} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

The converse fails.
$\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ of @exm-positive-definite is not positive definite,
yet it is invertible:
$\inv{\matr{D}} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.

:::
